Field notes · No. 3

The best source was on my vacation board

DJ, founderNovember 9, 20262 min read

I’ve been writing a talk about third places. The term comes from Ray Oldenburg’s 1989 book: the spots that aren’t home and aren’t work, where regulars gather. In New York that means the bodega with the cat, or the coffee counter where they start your order as you walk in.

My research board looked like every research board. Oldenburg on one card, the Wikipedia page on another. And the question I kept circling: can a visitor ever really get into someone else’s third place?

I had a hunch I’d seen an answer somewhere. Not in a paper. In a market.

So I pressed ⌘K and typed “Nishiki.”

The top result wasn’t from my research board at all. It was from the Kyoto trip, a lunch note I’d typed in a hurry: “Lunch at Nishiki: tamagoyaki, soy-milk donuts.” Opening it brought the whole afternoon back. The woman at the tamagoyaki stall greeted the man ahead of me by name, then turned to me and switched to English without missing a beat. Same warmth, different door.

That was my example. It had been sitting on a vacation board for a year.

I keep boards separate on purpose. A research board shouldn’t have to look at your packing list, and a trip board shouldn’t feel like homework. But your life doesn’t keep its ideas in separate folders. The good ones show up on the wrong board.

That’s what ⌘K in Nook is for. It searches every board at once, so the trip can answer the talk. I didn’t plan that cross-reference. I just wrote things down where they happened, and search found the thread later.

If you research anything, keep writing small notes on your other boards too. Some of them are sources. You just don’t know which ones yet.
